title: यूरोपका सडकमा उत्रिएका हजारौँ युवाले किन गाउँदैछन् १५५ वर्ष पुरानो ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ गीत ?
content:
No ads found for this position फ्रान्समा 'कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल' गीतको पुनरागमनले वर्तमान प्रदर्शनलाई ऐतिहासिक श्रमिक संघर्षसँग जोडेको छ, जहाँ विद्यार्थी र श्रमिक संगठनहरूले सरकारको बजेट कटौती र महँगीविरुद्ध आवाज उठाएका छन्। १८७१ मा लेखिएको यो गीत श्रमिक एकता, सामाजिक समानता र शोषणविरुद्धको संघर्षको प्रतीक मानिन्छ, र अहिलेको आन्दोलनमा यसको पुनः प्रयोगले युवापुस्ताको असन्तोषलाई ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भमा प्रस्तुत गरेको छ। युरोपका विभिन्न देशहरूमा आर्थिक असमानता र श्रमिक अधिकारका लागि भइरहेको आन्दोलनमा 'कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल' जस्तो ऐतिहासिक गीतले सामूहिक संघर्षको सन्देश दिन्छ । यसले आधुनिक राजनीतिक परिप्रेक्ष्यमा पुरानो विचारधारालाई पुनर्जीवित गरिरहेको छ । The return of the song "Communist Internationale" in France has linked current demonstrations to historic labor struggles, where students and labor organizations have spoken out against government budget cuts and inflation. Written in 1871, this song is considered a symbol of labor unity, social equality, and the struggle against exploitation, and its reuse in the current movement has placed the discontent of the younger generation in a historical context. In the ongoing struggles for economic inequality and workers' rights in various European countries, historic songs like 'Communist International' convey a message of collective struggle. It is reviving old ideologies in a modern political context. काठमाडौं । यूरोपका सडकमा अहिले एउटा पुरानो गीत फेरि सुनिन थालेको छ । झन्डै डेढ सय वर्षअघि लेखिएको क्रान्तिकारी गीत- ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल (International) । पेरिसमा प्रदर्शनकारीहरू एकै स्वरमा यो गीत गाइरहेका दृश्य सामाजिक सञ्जाल र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय सञ्चारमाध्यममा सार्वजनिक भइरहेका छन्। रातो झन्डा, विद्यार्थीका जुलुस, श्रमिक संगठनका प्रदर्शन र सरकारी नीतिविरुद्ध उठेका नाराबीच यो गीतको पुनरागमनले यूरोपको वर्तमान आन्दोलनलाई इतिहाससँग जोडेको छ । विद्यालयको अवस्था, बजेट कटौती र बढ्दो महँगीविरुद्ध देशव्यापी प्रदर्शन भइरहेका बेला माध्यमिक विद्यालयका विद्यार्थी, विश्वविद्यालयका विद्यार्थी तथा शिक्षक संगठनहरू आन्दोलनमा सहभागी भएका छन्। फ्रान्सेली अधिकारीहरूका अनुसार पेरिसबाहिर मंगलबार दिउँसोसम्म १४० वटा प्रदर्शनमा ३२ हजार ८ सय मानिस सहभागी भएका थिए। सरकारले आन्दोलनमा ‘अति वामपन्थी’ समूहको संलग्नता रहेको आरोप लगाएको छ । डेढ सय वर्ष पुरानो कम्युनिस्ट गीत गाएका कारण सरकारले यस्तो आरोप लगाएको हो । ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ श्रमिक एकता, सामाजिक समानता र शोषणविरुद्धको संघर्षको प्रतीक मानिने गीत हो। सन् १८७१ मा युजेन पोत्जिएले लेखेको यो गीत अहिले फेरि फ्रान्सका सडकमा गुञ्जिनुले वर्तमान आन्दोलनलाई ऐतिहासिक श्रमिक तथा क्रान्तिकारी संघर्षसँग जोडेको टिप्पणी गरिएको छ । महँगी, बेरोजगारी, आवास संकट, सार्वजनिक सेवामा बजेट कटौती र बढ्दो आर्थिक असमानताप्रति असन्तुष्ट नयाँ पुस्ताले विगतका क्रान्तिकारी प्रतीकलाई फेरि आफ्नो आन्दोलनको भाषाका रूपमा प्रयोग गरिरहेको संकेत यसलाई मानिएको छ । पेरिसमा किन गाइयो १५५ वर्ष पुरानो गीत ? नोभेम्बरमा फ्रान्सका विभिन्न सहरमा सरकारको आर्थिक नीति, बजेट कटौती, जीवनयापनको बढ्दो खर्च र शिक्षा क्षेत्रको अवस्थाविरुद्ध प्रदर्शन भइरहेका छन्। कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी, श्रमिक संगठन, विद्यार्थी समूह र वामपन्थी संगठनहरू यी प्रदर्शनमा सहभागी छन्। पेरिसको प्लास द ला रिपब्लिक (Place de la République) मा भएको प्रदर्शनमा सहभागीहरूले ऐतिहासिक क्रान्तिकारी गीत ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ सामूहिक रूपमा गाएको दृश्य सार्वजनिक भएको छ । यद्यपी यहाँ कम्युनिस्ट समूहभन्दा अन्य युवाहरूको सहभागिता बढी छ तर सबैले कम्युनिस्ट गीत गाएका छन् । यो गीत फ्रान्सेली कवि तथा क्रान्तिकारी युजेन पोत्जिए (Eugène Pottier) ले सन् १८७१ मा लेखेका थिए। त्यो समय फ्रान्सको इतिहासमा पेरिस कम्युनको छोटो तर प्रभावशाली क्रान्तिकारी प्रयोग भएको वर्ष थियो। पोत्जिए पेरिस कम्युनका समर्थक थिए । पेरिसमा मजदुर र क्रान्तिकारीहरूले सत्ता सञ्चालनको वैकल्पिक संरचना निर्माण गरेको उक्त ऐतिहासिक घटनापछि उनले लेखेको गीत श्रमिक वर्गको एकता, शोषणविरुद्ध विद्रोह र समानतामूलक समाज निर्माणको आकांक्षासँग जोडियो । गीतका शब्द लेखिएको केही वर्षपछि सन् १८८८ मा पियरे देगेतेर (Pierre De Geyter) ले यसको संगीत तयार पारे । त्यसपछि ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ फ्रान्सबाट बाहिर फैलिँदै विश्वभरका समाजवादी, कम्युनिस्ट र श्रमिक आन्दोलनको साझा गीत बन्न पुग्यो । आज पनि नेपालसहित संसारभरका कम्युनिस्ट पार्टीका औपचारिक समारोहमा यो गान गाइन्छ । यसले श्रमिकलाई आफ्नो वर्गीय एकता सम्झाउने, पुरानो सत्ता संरचनाविरुद्ध उठ्न प्रेरित गर्ने र समानताको सपना व्यक्त गर्ने सांस्कृतिक प्रतीकको रूप लिएका थियो । पेरिस कम्युनको स्मरण किन ? सन् १८७१ को पेरिस कम्युन आधुनिक राजनीतिक इतिहासको एउटा महत्त्वपूर्ण घटना हो । फ्रान्स-प्रुस युद्धपछि पेरिसमा उत्पन्न राजनीतिक संकटका बीच मजदुर, राष्ट्रिय गार्ड र क्रान्तिकारी शक्तिहरूले शहरमा आफ्नै शासन व्यवस्था सञ्चालन गरेका थिए। कम्युनले सामाजिक समानता, श्रमिकको अधिकार, धर्म र राज्यबीचको सम्बन्ध, सार्वजनिक सेवाको पुनर्संरचना तथा जनताको राजनीतिक सहभागिताजस्ता मुद्दा उठाएको थियो । तर त्यो शासन लामो समय टिकेन । फ्रान्सेली सरकारी सेनाले कम्युनलाई हिंसात्मक रूपमा दबायो । सन् १८७१ को मे महिनामा भएको दमनमा हजारौँ मानिस मारिए, गिरफ्तार भए वा निर्वासनमा पठाइए । पेरिस कम्युन त्यसपछि विश्वभरका समाजवादी र कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलनका लागि एउटा ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भ बन्यो । आज पनि विभिन्न ठाउँमा कम्युनहरुको अभ्यास गरिन्छ । कार्ल मार्क्सले पनि यसलाई मजदुर वर्गले राजनीतिक सत्ता प्रयोग गर्ने ऐतिहासिक अनुभवका रूपमा विश्लेषण गरेका थिए । आज पेरिसमा ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ गाउनु र कम्युनको स्मरण गर्नु वर्तमान आन्दोलनलाई त्यही ऐतिहासिक संघर्षको निरन्तरताका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्ने प्रतीकात्मक प्रयास भएको फ्रान्सेली कविहरुले बताएका छन् । मार्क्सको विचार फेरि सडकमा किन ? यूरोपका पछिल्ला आन्दोलनमा कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी, ट्रेड युनियन र विद्यार्थी संगठनहरूको सहभागिता उल्लेखनीय देखिएको छ । तर, प्रदर्शनमा सहभागी सबै युवा कम्युनिस्ट विचारधाराका अनुयायी हुन् भन्ने अर्थ लाग्दैन । किनकी यूरोपमा कम्युनिस्टहरूको संगठन अहिले त्यति निर्णायक मानिँदैन । अहिलेको आन्दोलनको प्रमुख आधार दैनिक जीवनसँग जोडिएका समस्या हुन् । महँगो घरभाडा, रोजगारीको असुरक्षा, बढ्दो मूल्य, सार्वजनिक शिक्षा र स्वास्थ्य सेवामा दबाब तथा सरकारको खर्च कटौती नीति। यस्ता समस्यालाई पूँजीवादी अर्थव्यवस्थाको असमानता र श्रमिकमाथिको शोषणसँग जोडेर व्याख्या गर्ने वामपन्थी संगठनहरूले आफ्ना ऐतिहासिक नारालाई पुनः अगाडि ल्याएका छन्। ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ त्यही राजनीतिक भाषाको एउटा प्रभावशाली प्रतीक हो । गीतले व्यक्तिगत असन्तुष्टिलाई सामूहिक संघर्षमा रूपान्तरण गर्ने सन्देश दिन्छ । त्यसैले अहिलेका प्रदर्शनमा यो गीत गाइनु आन्दोलनको राजनीतिक दिशा, इतिहाससँगको सम्बन्ध र एकताको सन्देश तीनवटै अर्थमा महत्त्वपूर्ण देखिन्छ। एथेन्समा कम्युनिस्ट विद्यार्थी र श्रमिकको मार्च ग्रीसको राजधानी एथेन्समा पनि कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी अफ ग्रीस (KKE) र त्यससँग सम्बद्ध श्रमिक संगठन PAME को नेतृत्वमा विद्यार्थी तथा श्रमिकहरूले प्रदर्शन गरेका छन् । प्रदर्शनमा रातो झन्डा, श्रमिक अधिकारका नारा र सरकारी आर्थिक नीतिविरुद्ध आवाज उठाइएको छ। एथेन्सका सडकमा देखिएका यस्ता जुलुसले यूरोपको दक्षिणी भागमा पनि श्रमिक र विद्यार्थी संगठनहरू आर्थिक तथा राजनीतिक मुद्दामा सक्रिय रहेको देखाउँछन्। ग्रीसको राजनीतिक इतिहासमा कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलनको बलियो उपस्थिति रहँदै आएको छ। आर्थिक संकट, बेरोजगारी र मितव्ययिताको नाममा लागू गरिएका कठोर नीतिहरूले विगतमा पनि त्यहाँ ठूलो जनआन्दोलन जन्माएका थिए । अहिलेको प्रदर्शनमा पुराना क्रान्तिकारी प्रतीकहरूको प्रयोगले त्यही इतिहासलाई नयाँ पुस्तामाझ पुनः स्थापित गर्ने प्रयास गरेको देखिन्छ। फ्रान्सदेखि स्पेनसम्म : आर्थिक असन्तुष्टिको साझा स्वर फ्रान्समा नोभेम्बर ५ र १७ मा ठूला प्रदर्शन तथा हड्ताल भएको विवरणहरू सार्वजनिक भएका छन् । स्पेनमा नोभेम्बर ११ मा आमहड्ताल, इटाली, जर्मनी र बेल्जियममा युवा प्रदर्शन तथा यूरोपका ३० भन्दा बढी देशमा विभिन्न स्वरूपका आन्दोलन भइरहेको रिपोर्टहरू आएका छन् । यी आन्दोलनका मुद्दा एउटै छैनन् । कतै सरकारको बजेट कटौतीविरुद्ध आवाज उठाइएको छ, कतै श्रमिकको तलब र अधिकारका लागि, कतै आवास संकट र महँगीविरुद्ध तथा कतै शिक्षा र सार्वजनिक सेवाको अवस्था सुधार्न माग गरिएको छ। तर, यी फरक मुद्दाबीच एउटा साझा असन्तुष्टि छ- आर्थिक विकासको लाभ समाजका सबै वर्गमा समान रूपमा नपुगेको र सामान्य नागरिकको जीवन झन् कठिन बन्दै गएको अनुभूति । यही असन्तुष्टिलाई वामपन्थी संगठनहरूले पूँजीवाद, वर्गीय असमानता र श्रमिक शोषणको प्रश्नसँग जोडिरहेका छन् । त्यसैले प्रदर्शनमा ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ जस्तो ऐतिहासिक गीतको पुनरागमनलाई केवल सांस्कृतिक घटना नभई राजनीतिक सन्देशका रूपमा पनि हेरिएको छ। १५५ वर्ष पुरानो गीत, नयाँ पुस्ताको आवाज ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ को मूल सन्देश श्रमिकको एकता र अन्यायपूर्ण व्यवस्था परिवर्तन गर्ने सामूहिक संघर्ष हो। गीतको चर्चित भावले श्रमिकहरूलाई पुरानो व्यवस्थाबाट मुक्ति खोज्न र आफ्नै भविष्य निर्माण गर्न आह्वान गर्छ । एक शताब्दीभन्दा बढी समय यो गीत विश्वका कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलन, समाजवादी पार्टी र श्रमिक संगठनहरूको साझा गान रह्यो। सोभियत संघलगायत विभिन्न देशमा यसले Kathmandu. An old song is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. The revolutionary song written almost 150 years ago - 'The Communist International'. Footage of protesters in Paris singing this song in unison is being made public on social media and international media. Amidst red flags, student marches, labor union demonstrations, and slogans raised against government policies, the song's return has connected Europe's current movements to history. As nationwide protests against school conditions, budget cuts, and rising inflation continue, secondary school students, university students, and teacher organizations have joined the movement. French authorities said 32,800 people had taken part in 140 demonstrations outside Paris by Tuesday afternoon. The government has accused the protests of being led by "far-left" groups, accusing them of singing a 150-year-old communist song. The Communist International is a song that symbolizes workers' unity, social equality, and the struggle against exploitation. Written by Eugene Potzier in 1871, this song is now resonating on the streets of France, connecting the current movement to historical workers' and revolutionary struggles. This is seen as a sign that a new generation, dissatisfied with inflation, unemployment, the housing crisis, budget cuts in public services, and growing economic inequality, is once again using the revolutionary symbols of the past as the language of their movement. Why was a 155-year-old song sung in Paris? In November, demonstrations are taking place in various cities across France against the government's economic policies, budget cuts, the rising cost of living, and the state of the education sector. The Communist Party, labor unions, student groups, and left-wing organizations are participating in these demonstrations. Footage has emerged of participants singing the historic revolutionary song 'The Internationale' en masse at a demonstration in Paris' Place de la République. Although the participation here is more from other youth groups than from communist groups, everyone is singing communist songs. This song was written by French poet and revolutionary Eugène Pottier in 1871. That was the year of the Paris Commune, a brief but influential revolutionary experiment in French history. Potzier was a supporter of the Paris Commune. After the historic event in which workers and revolutionaries created an alternative structure of power in Paris, the songs he wrote became associated with the unity of the working class, rebellion against exploitation, and aspirations for an egalitarian society. A few years after the lyrics were written, Pierre De Geyter composed the music for the song in 1888. The Internationale then spread beyond France and became a common anthem for socialist, communist, and labor movements around the world. Even today, the song is sung at official ceremonies of communist parties around the world, including Nepal. It took the form of a cultural symbol that reminded workers of their class unity, inspired them to rise up against the old power structure, and expressed the dream of equality. Why remember the Paris Commune? The Paris Commune of 1871 is a significant event in modern political history. Amid the political crisis that arose in Paris after the Franco-Prussian War, workers, National Guards, and revolutionary forces established their own government in the city. The commune raised issues such as social equality, workers' rights, the relationship between religion and state, the restructuring of public services, and the political participation of the people. But that rule did not last long. The French government troops violently suppressed the Commune. Thousands of people were killed, arrested, or sent into exile in the May 1871 crackdown. The Paris Commune then became a historical reference for socialist and communist movements around the world. Communes are still practiced in various places today. Karl Marx also analyzed it as a historical experience of the working class exercising political power. French poets have said that singing the 'Internationale' and remembering the Commune in Paris today is a symbolic attempt to present the current movement as a continuation of that historic struggle. Why are Marx's ideas on the streets again? The participation of communist parties, trade unions, and student organizations in recent movements in Europe has been notable. However, this does not mean that all the young people participating in the demonstrations are followers of communist ideology. Because the organization of communists in Europe is not considered to be that decisive at the moment. The main basis of the current movement is the problems related to daily life: high housing costs, job insecurity, rising prices, pressure on public education and health services, and government spending cuts. Leftist organizations that explain such problems by linking them to the inequality of the capitalist economy and the exploitation of workers have brought their historical slogans to the fore again. 'Communist International' is an influential symbol of that political language. The song conveys the message of transforming individual dissatisfaction into collective struggle. Therefore, singing this song in current demonstrations seems important in all three senses: the political direction of the movement, its connection to history, and its message of unity. March of communist students and workers in Athens Students and workers led by the Communist Party of Greece (KKE) and its affiliated labor organization PAME have also demonstrated in the Greek capital, Athens. The demonstrations, which have included red flags, workers' rights slogans and calls for a crackdown on government economic policies, are a sign that workers' and student organizations are also active on economic and political issues in southern Europe. The communist movement has had a strong presence in Greece's political history. Economic crisis, unemployment, and harsh policies implemented in the name of austerity have sparked large-scale popular movements there in the past. The use of old revolutionary symbols in the current demonstration appears to be an attempt to re-establish that same history among the new generation. From France to Spain: A common voice of economic discontent Reports of large demonstrations and strikes in France on November 5 and 17 have been released. There have been reports of a general strike in Spain on November 11, youth demonstrations in Italy, Germany and Belgium, and various forms of protests in more than 30 European countries. These movements are not all about the same issues. Some are against government budget cuts, others are for workers' wages and rights, others are against the housing crisis and inflation, and others are demanding improvements in education and public services. However, amidst these different issues, there is a common dissatisfaction - the feeling that the benefits of economic development are not reaching all sections of society equally and that the lives of ordinary citizens are becoming increasingly difficult. This discontent is being linked by left-wing organizations to questions of capitalism, class inequality, and labor exploitation. Therefore, the return of a historic song like the 'Internationale' to the demonstrations is seen not only as a cultural event but also as a political message. 155-year-old song, voice of a new generation The core message of the Communist International is the unity of workers and the collective struggle to change an unjust system. The song's famous lyrics call on workers to seek liberation from the old system and build their own future. For more than a century, this song has been the common anthem of communist movements, socialist parties, and labor organizations around the world. It has had a special place in national and political ceremonies in various countries, including the Soviet Union. In countries such as China, Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea, and Laos, communist regimes have given this song a place similar to the national anthem. Communist parties that have participated in central, provincial and local governments in countries including Nepal, India, Sri Lanka, Guinea, Cyprus, Peru and others at various times have sung the Communist International at their formal ceremonies. This song, written by Yutze Pottar in 1871, is probably the only song in the world that has been translated and set to music in the most languages. However, its return today does not only mean a desire to return to the political order of the past. Political analysts in Europe are commenting that it should also be understood as a cultural and political expression of the younger generation's attempt to connect their current dissatisfaction with historical struggles. The collective singing of protesters in videos from Paris that have spread on social media conveys the same message - even after decades of changing political systems, questions of economic inequality, workers' rights, and social justice have not gone away. The memory of the Paris Commune, the timeless ideas of Karl Marx, and the melody of the 'Communist International' are now being analyzed as a new crisis of capitalism, which is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. Whether this is a repetition of history or a new movement in which a new generation expresses its current dissatisfaction in the old revolutionary language - the political events of the coming days will answer that. हिंसात्मक रूपमा दबायो । सन् १८७१ को मे महिनामा भएको दमनमा हजारौँ मानिस मारिए, गिरफ्तार भए वा निर्वासनमा पठाइए । पेरिस कम्युन त्यसपछि विश्वभरका समाजवादी र कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलनका लागि एउटा ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भ बन्यो । आज पनि विभिन्न ठाउँमा कम्युनहरुको अभ्यास गरिन्छ । कार्ल मार्क्सले पनि यसलाई मजदुर वर्गले राजनीतिक सत्ता प्रयोग गर्ने ऐतिहासिक अनुभवका रूपमा विश्लेषण गरेका थिए । आज पेरिसमा ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ Kathmandu. An old song is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. The revolutionary song written almost 150 years ago - 'The Communist International'. Footage of protesters in Paris singing this song in unison is being made public on social media and international media. Amidst red flags, student marches, labor union demonstrations, and slogans raised against government policies, the song's return has connected Europe's current movements to history. As nationwide protests against school conditions, budget cuts, and rising inflation continue, secondary school students, university students, and teacher organizations have joined the movement. French authorities said 32,800 people had taken part in 140 demonstrations outside Paris by Tuesday afternoon. The government has accused the protests of being led by "far-left" groups, accusing them of singing a 150-year-old communist song. The Communist International is a song that symbolizes workers' unity, social equality, and the struggle against exploitation. Written by Eugene Potzier in 1871, this song is now resonating on the streets of France, connecting the current movement to historical workers' and revolutionary struggles. This is seen as a sign that a new generation, dissatisfied with inflation, unemployment, the housing crisis, budget cuts in public services, and growing economic inequality, is once again using the revolutionary symbols of the past as the language of their movement. Why was a 155-year-old song sung in Paris? In November, demonstrations are taking place in various cities across France against the government's economic policies, budget cuts, the rising cost of living, and the state of the education sector. The Communist Party, labor unions, student groups, and left-wing organizations are participating in these demonstrations. Footage has emerged of participants singing the historic revolutionary song 'The Internationale' en masse at a demonstration in Paris' Place de la République. Although the participation here is more from other youth groups than from communist groups, everyone is singing communist songs. This song was written by French poet and revolutionary Eugène Pottier in 1871. That was the year of the Paris Commune, a brief but influential revolutionary experiment in French history. Potzier was a supporter of the Paris Commune. After the historic event in which workers and revolutionaries created an alternative structure of power in Paris, the songs he wrote became associated with the unity of the working class, rebellion against exploitation, and aspirations for an egalitarian society. A few years after the lyrics were written, Pierre De Geyter composed the music for the song in 1888. The Internationale then spread beyond France and became a common anthem for socialist, communist, and labor movements around the world. Even today, the song is sung at official ceremonies of communist parties around the world, including Nepal. It took the form of a cultural symbol that reminded workers of their class unity, inspired them to rise up against the old power structure, and expressed the dream of equality. Why remember the Paris Commune? The Paris Commune of 1871 is a significant event in modern political history. Amid the political crisis that arose in Paris after the Franco-Prussian War, workers, National Guards, and revolutionary forces established their own government in the city. The commune raised issues such as social equality, workers' rights, the relationship between religion and state, the restructuring of public services, and the political participation of the people. But that rule did not last long. The French government troops violently suppressed the Commune. Thousands of people were killed, arrested, or sent into exile in the May 1871 crackdown. The Paris Commune then became a historical reference for socialist and communist movements around the world. Communes are still practiced in various places today. Karl Marx also analyzed it as a historical experience of the working class exercising political power. French poets have said that singing the 'Internationale' and remembering the Commune in Paris today is a symbolic attempt to present the current movement as a continuation of that historic struggle. Why are Marx's ideas on the streets again? The participation of communist parties, trade unions, and student organizations in recent movements in Europe has been notable. However, this does not mean that all the young people participating in the demonstrations are followers of communist ideology. Because the organization of communists in Europe is not considered to be that decisive at the moment. The main basis of the current movement is the problems related to daily life: high housing costs, job insecurity, rising prices, pressure on public education and health services, and government spending cuts. Leftist organizations that explain such problems by linking them to the inequality of the capitalist economy and the exploitation of workers have brought their historical slogans to the fore again. 'Communist International' is an influential symbol of that political language. The song conveys the message of transforming individual dissatisfaction into collective struggle. Therefore, singing this song in current demonstrations seems important in all three senses: the political direction of the movement, its connection to history, and its message of unity. March of communist students and workers in Athens Students and workers led by the Communist Party of Greece (KKE) and its affiliated labor organization PAME have also demonstrated in the Greek capital, Athens. The demonstrations, which have included red flags, workers' rights slogans and calls for a crackdown on government economic policies, are a sign that workers' and student organizations are also active on economic and political issues in southern Europe. The communist movement has had a strong presence in Greece's political history. Economic crisis, unemployment, and harsh policies implemented in the name of austerity have sparked large-scale popular movements there in the past. The use of old revolutionary symbols in the current demonstration appears to be an attempt to re-establish that same history among the new generation. From France to Spain: A common voice of economic discontent Reports of large demonstrations and strikes in France on November 5 and 17 have been released. There have been reports of a general strike in Spain on November 11, youth demonstrations in Italy, Germany and Belgium, and various forms of protests in more than 30 European countries. These movements are not all about the same issues. Some are against government budget cuts, others are for workers' wages and rights, others are against the housing crisis and inflation, and others are demanding improvements in education and public services. However, amidst these different issues, there is a common dissatisfaction - the feeling that the benefits of economic development are not reaching all sections of society equally and that the lives of ordinary citizens are becoming increasingly difficult. This discontent is being linked by left-wing organizations to questions of capitalism, class inequality, and labor exploitation. Therefore, the return of a historic song like the 'Internationale' to the demonstrations is seen not only as a cultural event but also as a political message. 155-year-old song, voice of a new generation The core message of the Communist International is the unity of workers and the collective struggle to change an unjust system. The song's famous lyrics call on workers to seek liberation from the old system and build their own future. For more than a century, this song has been the common anthem of communist movements, socialist parties, and labor organizations around the world. It has had a special place in national and political ceremonies in various countries, including the Soviet Union. In countries such as China, Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea, and Laos, communist regimes have given this song a place similar to the national anthem. Communist parties that have participated in central, provincial and local governments in countries including Nepal, India, Sri Lanka, Guinea, Cyprus, Peru and others at various times have sung the Communist International at their formal ceremonies. This song, written by Yutze Pottar in 1871, is probably the only song in the world that has been translated and set to music in the most languages. However, its return today does not only mean a desire to return to the political order of the past. Political analysts in Europe are commenting that it should also be understood as a cultural and political expression of the younger generation's attempt to connect their current dissatisfaction with historical struggles. The collective singing of protesters in videos from Paris that have spread on social media conveys the same message - even after decades of changing political systems, questions of economic inequality, workers' rights, and social justice have not gone away. The memory of the Paris Commune, the timeless ideas of Karl Marx, and the melody of the 'Communist International' are now being analyzed as a new crisis of capitalism, which is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. Whether this is a repetition of history or a new movement in which a new generation expresses its current dissatisfaction in the old revolutionary language - the political events of the coming days will answer that. एकता, सामाजिक समानता र शोषणविरुद्धको संघर्षको प्रतीक मानिने गीत हो। सन् १८७१ मा युजेन पोत्जिएले लेखेको यो गीत अहिले फेरि फ्रान्सका सडकमा गुञ्जिनुले वर्तमान आन्दोलनलाई ऐतिहासिक श्रमिक तथा क्रान्तिकारी संघर्षसँग जोडेको टिप्पणी गरिएको छ । महँगी, बेरोजगारी, आवास संकट, सार्वजनिक सेवामा बजेट कटौती र बढ्दो आर्थिक असमानताप्रति असन्तुष्ट नयाँ पुस्ताले विगतका क्रान्तिकारी प्रतीकलाई फेरि आफ्नो आन्दोलनको भाषाका रूपमा प्रयोग गरिरहेको संकेत यसलाई मानिएको छ । पेरिसमा किन गाइयो १५५ वर्ष पुरानो गीत ? नोभेम्बरमा फ्रान्सका विभिन्न सहरमा सरकारको आर्थिक नीति, बजेट कटौती, जीवनयापनको बढ्दो खर्च र शिक्षा क्षेत्रको अवस्थाविरुद्ध प्रदर्शन भइरहेका छन्। कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी, श्रमिक संगठन, विद्यार्थी समूह र वामपन्थी संगठनहरू यी प्रदर्शनमा सहभागी छन्। पेरिसको प्लास द ला रिपब्लिक (Place de la République) मा भएको प्रदर्शनमा सहभागीहरूले ऐतिहासिक क्रान्तिकारी गीत ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ सामूहिक रूपमा गाएको दृश्य सार्वजनिक भएको छ । यद्यपी यहाँ कम्युनिस्ट समूहभन्दा अन्य युवाहरूको सहभागिता बढी छ तर सबैले कम्युनिस्ट गीत गाएका छन् । यो गीत फ्रान्सेली कवि तथा क्रान्तिकारी युजेन पोत्जिए (Eugène Pottier) ले सन् १८७१ मा लेखेका थिए। त्यो समय फ्रान्सको इतिहासमा पेरिस कम्युनको छोटो तर प्रभावशाली क्रान्तिकारी प्रयोग भएको वर्ष थियो। पोत्जिए पेरिस कम्युनका समर्थक थिए । पेरिसमा मजदुर र क्रान्तिकारीहरूले सत्ता सञ्चालनको वैकल्पिक संरचना निर्माण गरेको उक्त ऐतिहासिक घटनापछि उनले लेखेको गीत श्रमिक वर्गको एकता, शोषणविरुद्ध विद्रोह र समानतामूलक समाज निर्माणको आकांक्षासँग जोडियो । गीतका शब्द लेखिएको केही वर्षपछि सन् १८८८ मा पियरे देगेतेर (Pierre De Geyter) ले यसको संगीत तयार पारे । त्यसपछि ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ फ्रान्सबाट बाहिर फैलिँदै विश्वभरका समाजवादी, कम्युनिस्ट र श्रमिक आन्दोलनको साझा गीत बन्न पुग्यो । आज पनि नेपालसहित संसारभरका कम्युनिस्ट पार्टीका औपचारिक समारोहमा यो गान गाइन्छ । यसले श्रमिकलाई आफ्नो वर्गीय एकता सम्झाउने, पुरानो सत्ता संरचनाविरुद्ध उठ्न प्रेरित गर्ने र समानताको सपना व्यक्त गर्ने सांस्कृतिक प्रतीकको रूप लिएका थियो । पेरिस कम्युनको स्मरण किन ? सन् १८७१ को पेरिस कम्युन आधुनिक राजनीतिक इतिहासको एउटा महत्त्वपूर्ण घटना हो । फ्रान्स-प्रुस युद्धपछि पेरिसमा उत्पन्न राजनीतिक संकटका बीच मजदुर, राष्ट्रिय गार्ड र क्रान्तिकारी शक्तिहरूले शहरमा आफ्नै शासन व्यवस्था सञ्चालन गरेका थिए। कम्युनले सामाजिक समानता, श्रमिकको अधिकार, धर्म र राज्यबीचको सम्बन्ध, सार्वजनिक सेवाको पुनर्संरचना तथा जनताको राजनीतिक सहभागिताजस्ता मुद्दा उठाएको थियो । तर त्यो शासन लामो समय टिकेन । फ्रान्सेली सरकारी सेनाले कम्युनलाई हिंसात्मक रूपमा दबायो । सन् १८७१ को मे महिनामा भएको दमनमा हजारौँ मानिस मारिए, गिरफ्तार भए वा निर्वासनमा पठाइए । पेरिस कम्युन त्यसपछि विश्वभरका समाजवादी र कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलनका लागि एउटा ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भ बन्यो । आज पनि विभिन्न ठाउँमा कम्युनहरुको अभ्यास गरिन्छ । कार्ल मार्क्सले पनि यसलाई मजदुर वर्गले राजनीतिक सत्ता प्रयोग गर्ने ऐतिहासिक अनुभवका रूपमा विश्लेषण गरेका थिए । आज पेरिसमा ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ गाउनु र कम्युनको स्मरण गर्नु वर्तमान आन्दोलनलाई त्यही ऐतिहासिक संघर्षको निरन्तरताका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्ने प्रतीकात्मक प्रयास भएको फ्रान्सेली कविहरुले बताएका छन् । मार्क्सको विचार फेरि सडकमा किन ? यूरोपका पछिल्ला आन्दोलनमा कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी, ट्रेड युनियन र विद्यार्थी संगठनहरूको सहभागिता उल्लेखनीय देखिएको छ । तर, प्रदर्शनमा सहभागी सबै युवा कम्युनिस्ट विचारधाराका अनुयायी हुन् भन्ने अर्थ लाग्दैन । किनकी यूरोपमा कम्युनिस्टहरूको संगठन अहिले त्यति निर्णायक मानिँदैन । अहिलेको आन्दोलनको प्रमुख आधार दैनिक जीवनसँग जोडिएका समस्या हुन् । महँगो घरभाडा, रोजगारीको असुरक्षा, बढ्दो मूल्य, सार्वजनिक शिक्षा र स्वास्थ्य सेवामा दबाब तथा सरकारको खर्च कटौती नीति। यस्ता समस्यालाई पूँजीवादी अर्थव्यवस्थाको असमानता र श्रमिकमाथिको शोषणसँग जोडेर व्याख्या गर्ने वामपन्थी संगठनहरूले आफ्ना ऐतिहासिक नारालाई पुनः अगाडि ल्याएका छन्। ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ त्यही राजनीतिक भाषाको एउटा प्रभावशाली प्रतीक हो । गीतले व्यक्तिगत असन्तुष्टिलाई सामूहिक संघर्षमा रूपान्तरण गर्ने सन्देश दिन्छ । त्यसैले अहिलेका प्रदर्शनमा यो गीत गाइनु आन्दोलनको राजनीतिक दिशा, इतिहाससँगको सम्बन्ध र एकताको सन्देश तीनवटै अर्थमा महत्त्वपूर्ण देखिन्छ। एथेन्समा कम्युनिस्ट विद्यार्थी र श्रमिकको मार्च ग्रीसको राजधानी एथेन्समा पनि कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी अफ ग्रीस (KKE) र त्यससँग सम्बद्ध श्रमिक संगठन PAME को नेतृत्वमा विद्यार्थी तथा श्रमिकहरूले प्रदर्शन गरेका छन् । प्रदर्शनमा रातो झन्डा, श्रमिक अधिकारका नारा र सरकारी आर्थिक नीतिविरुद्ध आवाज उठाइएको छ। एथेन्सका सडकमा देखिएका यस्ता जुलुसले यूरोपको दक्षिणी भागमा पनि श्रमिक र विद्यार्थी संगठनहरू आर्थिक तथा राजनीतिक मुद्दामा सक्रिय रहेको देखाउँछन्। ग्रीसको राजनीतिक इतिहासमा कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलनको बलियो उपस्थिति रहँदै आएको छ। आर्थिक संकट, बेरोजगारी र मितव्ययिताको नाममा लागू गरिएका कठोर नीतिहरूले विगतमा पनि त्यहाँ ठूलो जनआन्दोलन जन्माएका थिए । अहिलेको प्रदर्शनमा पुराना क्रान्तिकारी प्रतीकहरूको प्रयोगले त्यही इतिहासलाई नयाँ पुस्तामाझ पुनः स्थापित गर्ने प्रयास गरेको देखिन्छ। फ्रान्सदेखि स्पेनसम्म : आर्थिक असन्तुष्टिको साझा स्वर फ्रान्समा नोभेम्बर ५ र १७ मा ठूला प्रदर्शन तथा हड्ताल भएको विवरणहरू सार्वजनिक भएका छन् । स्पेनमा नोभेम्बर ११ मा आमहड्ताल, इटाली, जर्मनी र बेल्जियममा युवा प्रदर्शन तथा यूरोपका ३० भन्दा बढी देशमा विभिन्न स्वरूपका आन्दोलन भइरहेको रिपोर्टहरू आएका छन् । यी आन्दोलनका मुद्दा एउटै छैनन् । कतै सरकारको बजेट कटौतीविरुद्ध आवाज उठाइएको छ, कतै श्रमिकको तलब र अधिकारका लागि, कतै आवास संकट र महँगीविरुद्ध तथा कतै शिक्षा र सार्वजनिक सेवाको अवस्था सुधार्न माग गरिएको छ। तर, यी फरक मुद्दाबीच एउटा साझा असन्तुष्टि छ- आर्थिक विकासको लाभ समाजका सबै वर्गमा समान रूपमा नपुगेको र सामान्य नागरिकको जीवन झन् कठिन बन्दै गएको अनुभूति । यही असन्तुष्टिलाई वामपन्थी संगठनहरूले पूँजीवाद, वर्गीय असमानता र श्रमिक शोषणको प्रश्नसँग जोडिरहेका छन् । त्यसैले प्रदर्शनमा ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ जस्तो ऐतिहासिक गीतको पुनरागमनलाई केवल सांस्कृतिक घटना नभई राजनीतिक सन्देशका रूपमा पनि हेरिएको छ। १५५ वर्ष पुरानो गीत, नयाँ पुस्ताको आवाज ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ को मूल सन्देश श्रमिकको एकता र अन्यायपूर्ण व्यवस्था परिवर्तन गर्ने सामूहिक संघर्ष हो। गीतको चर्चित भावले श्रमिकहरूलाई पुरानो व्यवस्थाबाट मुक्ति खोज्न र आफ्नै भविष्य निर्माण गर्न आह्वान गर्छ । एक शताब्दीभन्दा बढी समय यो गीत विश्वका कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलन, समाजवादी पार्टी र श्रमिक संगठनहरूको साझा गान रह्यो। सोभियत संघलगायत विभिन्न देशमा यसले राष्ट्रिय तथा राजनीतिक समारोहमा विशेष स्थान पाएको थियो । चीन,भियतनाम,क्युवा,उत्तर कोरिया,लाओसजस्ता देशमा कम्युनिस्ट सत्ताले यो गीतलाई अहिले पनि राष्ट्रिय गानजत्तिकै स्थान दिएका छन् । नेपाल,भारत,श्रीलंका,किनारागुवा,साइप्रस,पेरु लगायतका देशमा विभिन्न समयमा केन्द्र तथा प्रदेश र स्थानीय सरकारमा सहभागिता जनाएका कम्युनिस्ट पार्टीहरूले आफ्ना औपचारिक समारोहहरूमा कम्युनिस्ट अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय गाउने गरेका छन् । सन् १८७१ मा युत्जे पोत्तरले लेखेको यो गीत सम्भवतः संसारमा सबैभन्दा धेरै भाषामा अनुवादित र संगीतबद्ध गरिएको एकमात्र गीत हो । तर, आज यसको पुनरागमनको अर्थ विगतकै राजनीतिक व्यवस्था Kathmandu. An old song is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. The revolutionary song written almost 150 years ago - 'The Communist International'. Footage of protesters in Paris singing this song in unison is being made public on social media and international media. Amidst red flags, student marches, labor union demonstrations, and slogans raised against government policies, the song's return has connected Europe's current movements to history. As nationwide protests against school conditions, budget cuts, and rising inflation continue, secondary school students, university students, and teacher organizations have joined the movement. French authorities said 32,800 people had taken part in 140 demonstrations outside Paris by Tuesday afternoon. The government has accused the protests of being led by "far-left" groups, accusing them of singing a 150-year-old communist song. The Communist International is a song that symbolizes workers' unity, social equality, and the struggle against exploitation. Written by Eugene Potzier in 1871, this song is now resonating on the streets of France, connecting the current movement to historical workers' and revolutionary struggles. This is seen as a sign that a new generation, dissatisfied with inflation, unemployment, the housing crisis, budget cuts in public services, and growing economic inequality, is once again using the revolutionary symbols of the past as the language of their movement. Why was a 155-year-old song sung in Paris? In November, demonstrations are taking place in various cities across France against the government's economic policies, budget cuts, the rising cost of living, and the state of the education sector. The Communist Party, labor unions, student groups, and left-wing organizations are participating in these demonstrations. Footage has emerged of participants singing the historic revolutionary song 'The Internationale' en masse at a demonstration in Paris' Place de la République. Although the participation here is more from other youth groups than from communist groups, everyone is singing communist songs. This song was written by French poet and revolutionary Eugène Pottier in 1871. That was the year of the Paris Commune, a brief but influential revolutionary experiment in French history. Potzier was a supporter of the Paris Commune. After the historic event in which workers and revolutionaries created an alternative structure of power in Paris, the songs he wrote became associated with the unity of the working class, rebellion against exploitation, and aspirations for an egalitarian society. A few years after the lyrics were written, Pierre De Geyter composed the music for the song in 1888. The Internationale then spread beyond France and became a common anthem for socialist, communist, and labor movements around the world. Even today, the song is sung at official ceremonies of communist parties around the world, including Nepal. It took the form of a cultural symbol that reminded workers of their class unity, inspired them to rise up against the old power structure, and expressed the dream of equality. Why remember the Paris Commune? The Paris Commune of 1871 is a significant event in modern political history. Amid the political crisis that arose in Paris after the Franco-Prussian War, workers, National Guards, and revolutionary forces established their own government in the city. The commune raised issues such as social equality, workers' rights, the relationship between religion and state, the restructuring of public services, and the political participation of the people. But that rule did not last long. The French government troops violently suppressed the Commune. Thousands of people were killed, arrested, or sent into exile in the May 1871 crackdown. The Paris Commune then became a historical reference for socialist and communist movements around the world. Communes are still practiced in various places today. Karl Marx also analyzed it as a historical experience of the working class exercising political power. French poets have said that singing the 'Internationale' and remembering the Commune in Paris today is a symbolic attempt to present the current movement as a continuation of that historic struggle. Why are Marx's ideas on the streets again? The participation of communist parties, trade unions, and student organizations in recent movements in Europe has been notable. However, this does not mean that all the young people participating in the demonstrations are followers of communist ideology. Because the organization of communists in Europe is not considered to be that decisive at the moment. The main basis of the current movement is the problems related to daily life: high housing costs, job insecurity, rising prices, pressure on public education and health services, and government spending cuts. Leftist organizations that explain such problems by linking them to the inequality of the capitalist economy and the exploitation of workers have brought their historical slogans to the fore again. 'Communist International' is an influential symbol of that political language. The song conveys the message of transforming individual dissatisfaction into collective struggle. Therefore, singing this song in current demonstrations seems important in all three senses: the political direction of the movement, its connection to history, and its message of unity. March of communist students and workers in Athens Students and workers led by the Communist Party of Greece (KKE) and its affiliated labor organization PAME have also demonstrated in the Greek capital, Athens. The demonstrations, which have included red flags, workers' rights slogans and calls for a crackdown on government economic policies, are a sign that workers' and student organizations are also active on economic and political issues in southern Europe. The communist movement has had a strong presence in Greece's political history. Economic crisis, unemployment, and harsh policies implemented in the name of austerity have sparked large-scale popular movements there in the past. The use of old revolutionary symbols in the current demonstration appears to be an attempt to re-establish that same history among the new generation. From France to Spain: A common voice of economic discontent Reports of large demonstrations and strikes in France on November 5 and 17 have been released. There have been reports of a general strike in Spain on November 11, youth demonstrations in Italy, Germany and Belgium, and various forms of protests in more than 30 European countries. These movements are not all about the same issues. Some are against government budget cuts, others are for workers' wages and rights, others are against the housing crisis and inflation, and others are demanding improvements in education and public services. However, amidst these different issues, there is a common dissatisfaction - the feeling that the benefits of economic development are not reaching all sections of society equally and that the lives of ordinary citizens are becoming increasingly difficult. This discontent is being linked by left-wing organizations to questions of capitalism, class inequality, and labor exploitation. Therefore, the return of a historic song like the 'Internationale' to the demonstrations is seen not only as a cultural event but also as a political message. 155-year-old song, voice of a new generation The core message of the Communist International is the unity of workers and the collective struggle to change an unjust system. The song's famous lyrics call on workers to seek liberation from the old system and build their own future. For more than a century, this song has been the common anthem of communist movements, socialist parties, and labor organizations around the world. It has had a special place in national and political ceremonies in various countries, including the Soviet Union. In countries such as China, Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea, and Laos, communist regimes have given this song a place similar to the national anthem. Communist parties that have participated in central, provincial and local governments in countries including Nepal, India, Sri Lanka, Guinea, Cyprus, Peru and others at various times have sung the Communist International at their formal ceremonies. This song, written by Yutze Pottar in 1871, is probably the only song in the world that has been translated and set to music in the most languages. However, its return today does not only mean a desire to return to the political order of the past. Political analysts in Europe are commenting that it should also be understood as a cultural and political expression of the younger generation's attempt to connect their current dissatisfaction with historical struggles. The collective singing of protesters in videos from Paris that have spread on social media conveys the same message - even after decades of changing political systems, questions of economic inequality, workers' rights, and social justice have not gone away. The memory of the Paris Commune, the timeless ideas of Karl Marx, and the melody of the 'Communist International' are now being analyzed as a new crisis of capitalism, which is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. Whether this is a repetition of history or a new movement in which a new generation expresses its current dissatisfaction in the old revolutionary language - the political events of the coming days will answer that. Kathmandu. An old song is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. The revolutionary song written almost 150 years ago - 'The Communist International'. Footage of protesters in Paris singing this song in unison is being made public on social media and international media. Amidst red flags, student marches, labor union demonstrations, and slogans raised against government policies, the song's return has connected Europe's current movements to history. As nationwide protests against school conditions, budget cuts, and rising inflation continue, secondary school students, university students, and teacher organizations have joined the movement. French authorities said 32,800 people had taken part in 140 demonstrations outside Paris by Tuesday afternoon. The government has accused the protests of being led by "far-left" groups, accusing them of singing a 150-year-old communist song. The Communist International is a song that symbolizes workers' unity, social equality, and the struggle against exploitation. Written by Eugene Potzier in 1871, this song is now resonating on the streets of France, connecting the current movement to historical workers' and revolutionary struggles. This is seen as a sign that a new generation, dissatisfied with inflation, unemployment, the housing crisis, budget cuts in public services, and growing economic inequality, is once again using the revolutionary symbols of the past as the language of their movement. Why was a 155-year-old song sung in Paris? In November, demonstrations are taking place in various cities across France against the government's economic policies, budget cuts, the rising cost of living, and the state of the education sector. The Communist Party, labor unions, student groups, and left-wing organizations are participating in these demonstrations. Footage has emerged of participants singing the historic revolutionary song 'The Internationale' en masse at a demonstration in Paris' Place de la République. Although the participation here is more from other youth groups than from communist groups, everyone is singing communist songs. This song was written by French poet and revolutionary Eugène Pottier in 1871. That was the year of the Paris Commune, a brief but influential revolutionary experiment in French history. Potzier was a supporter of the Paris Commune. After the historic event in which workers and revolutionaries created an alternative structure of power in Paris, the songs he wrote became associated with the unity of the working class, rebellion against exploitation, and aspirations for an egalitarian society. A few years after the lyrics were written, Pierre De Geyter composed the music for the song in 1888. The Internationale then spread beyond France and became a common anthem for socialist, communist, and labor movements around the world. Even today, the song is sung at official ceremonies of communist parties around the world, including Nepal. It took the form of a cultural symbol that reminded workers of their class unity, inspired them to rise up against the old power structure, and expressed the dream of equality. Why remember the Paris Commune? The Paris Commune of 1871 is a significant event in modern political history. Amid the political crisis that arose in Paris after the Franco-Prussian War, workers, National Guards, and revolutionary forces established their own government in the city. The commune raised issues such as social equality, workers' rights, the relationship between religion and state, the restructuring of public services, and the political participation of the people. But that rule did not last long. The French government troops violently suppressed the Commune. Thousands of people were killed, arrested, or sent into exile in the May 1871 crackdown. The Paris Commune then became a historical reference for socialist and communist movements around the world. Communes are still practiced in various places today. Karl Marx also analyzed it as a historical experience of the working class exercising political power. French poets have said that singing the 'Internationale' and remembering the Commune in Paris today is a symbolic attempt to present the current movement as a continuation of that historic struggle. Why are Marx's ideas on the streets again? The participation of communist parties, trade unions, and student organizations in recent movements in Europe has been notable. However, this does not mean that all the young people participating in the demonstrations are followers of communist ideology. Because the organization of communists in Europe is not considered to be that decisive at the moment. The main basis of the current movement is the problems related to daily life: high housing costs, job insecurity, rising prices, pressure on public education and health services, and government spending cuts. Leftist organizations that explain such problems by linking them to the inequality of the capitalist economy and the exploitation of workers have brought their historical slogans to the fore again. 'Communist International' is an influential symbol of that political language. The song conveys the message of transforming individual dissatisfaction into collective struggle. Therefore, singing this song in current demonstrations seems important in all three senses: the political direction of the movement, its connection to history, and its message of unity. आवाज उठाइएको छ, कतै श्रमिकको तलब र अधिकारका लागि, कतै आवास संकट र महँगीविरुद्ध तथा कतै शिक्षा र सार्वजनिक सेवाको अवस्था सुधार्न माग गरिएको छ। तर, यी फरक मुद्दाबीच एउटा साझा असन्तुष्टि छ- आर्थिक विकासको लाभ समाजका सबै वर्गमा समान रूपमा नपुगेको र सामान्य नागरिकको जीवन झन् कठिन बन्दै गएको अनुभूति । यही असन्तुष्टिलाई वामपन्थी संगठनहरूले पूँजीवाद, वर्गीय असमानता र श्रमिक शोषणको प्रश्नसँग जोडिरहेका छन् । त्यसैले प्रदर्शनमा ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ जस्तो ऐतिहासिक गीतको पुनरागमनलाई केवल सांस्कृतिक घटना नभई राजनीतिक सन्देशका रूपमा पनि हेरिएको छ। १५५ वर्ष पुरानो गीत, नयाँ पुस्ताको आवाज ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ को मूल सन्देश श्रमिकको एकता र अन्यायपूर्ण व्यवस्था परिवर्तन गर्ने सामूहिक संघर्ष हो। गीतको चर्चित भावले श्रमिकहरूलाई पुरानो व्यवस्थाबाट मुक्ति खोज्न र आफ्नै भविष्य निर्माण गर्न आह्वान गर्छ । एक शताब्दीभन्दा बढी समय यो गीत विश्वका कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलन, समाजवादी पार्टी र श्रमिक संगठनहरूको साझा गान रह्यो। सोभियत संघलगायत विभिन्न देशमा यसले राष्ट्रिय तथा राजनीतिक समारोहमा विशेष स्थान पाएको थियो । चीन,भियतनाम,क्युवा,उत्तर कोरिया,लाओसजस्ता देशमा कम्युनिस्ट सत्ताले यो गीतलाई अहिले पनि राष्ट्रिय गानजत्तिकै स्थान दिएका छन् । नेपाल,भारत,श्रीलंका,किनारागुवा,साइप्रस,पेरु लगायतका देशमा विभिन्न समयमा केन्द्र तथा प्रदेश र स्थानीय सरकारमा सहभागिता जनाएका कम्युनिस्ट पार्टीहरूले आफ्ना औपचारिक समारोहहरूमा कम्युनिस्ट अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय गाउने गरेका छन् । सन् १८७१ मा युत्जे पोत्तरले लेखेको यो गीत सम्भवतः संसारमा सबैभन्दा धेरै भाषामा अनुवादित र संगीतबद्ध गरिएको एकमात्र गीत हो । तर, आज यसको पुनरागमनको अर्थ विगतकै राजनीतिक व्यवस्था फर्काउने चाहना मात्रै होइन । युवा पुस्ताले आफ्नो वर्तमान असन्तुष्टिलाई इतिहासका संघर्षसँग जोड्न खोजेको सांस्कृतिक र राजनीतिक अभिव्यक्तिका रुपमा पनि बुझ्नुपर्ने यूरोपका राजनीतिक विश्लेषकले टिप्पणी गरिरहेका छन् । सामाजिक सञ्जालमा फैलिएका पेरिसका भिडियोहरूमा प्रदर्शनकारीहरूको सामूहिक गायनले यही सन्देश दिन्छ-राजनीतिक व्यवस्था बदलिएको दशकौँपछि पनि आर्थिक असमानता, श्रमिक अधिकार र सामाजिक न्यायका प्रश्नहरू समाप्त भएका छैनन्। पेरिस कम्युनको सम्झना, कार्ल माक्र्सको कालजयी विचार र ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ को धुन अहिले यूरोपका सडकमा फेरि सुनिन थाल्नु पुँजिवादको नयाँ संकटका रूपमा पनि विश्लेषण गरिँदैछ । यो कुरा इतिहासको पुनरावृत्ति हो वा नयाँ पुस्ताले पुरानो क्रान्तिकारी भाषामा आफ्नो वर्तमान असन्तुष्टि व्यक्त गरेको नयाँ आन्दोलन- त्यसको जवाफ आगामी दिनका राजनीतिक घटनाक्रमले दिनेछन् । सन् १८७१ मा युँजे पोत्तरले लेखेको कम्युनिस्ट अन्तर्राष्ट्रियको नेपाली अनुवाद यस्तो छ– यूजें पोत्तरले लेखेको कम्युनिष्ट अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय गीत १ उठ, जाग, हे ! भोकानाङ्गा, जाग संसारका दुःखी सुन्दर संसार रचना गर्न, न्यायको लागि गर्जी बाध्नेछैन परम्पराको साङ्लोले जाग, ए श्रमिक हो ! नयाँ जगमा पृथ्वी उठ्ने छ र सारा संसार हाम्रो हुने छ । यो अन्तिम युद्ध हो आ–आफ्नो ठाउँमा डटौं अब मानिसको अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय जाति हुने छ यो अन्तिम युद्ध हो आ–आफ्नो ठाउँमा डटौं अब मानिसको अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय जाति हुने छ । २ तिनको अदालतबाट शासित हुन हामी चाहन्नौं तिनको कृपालाई कुल्चदैँ बरु सबै भई सल्लाह गरौं लुटाहाबाट आफ्नो धन खोस्न, शोषणबाट मुक्त हुन आफ्नो कर्तब्य आफैँले, निर्णय गरी पूरा गर्न यो अन्तिम युद्ध हो ३ ज्यामी खेताला एक भई आऊ, श्रमिकहरूको संघमा धर्ती हामी श्रमिकको हो, होइन जालीझेली काँतरको मोटाए यी कयौं हाम्रो रगत मासुले तर ती हत्यारा कुनै बिहान नष्ट हुनेछन् र उज्यालो रहिरहने छ । यो अन्तिम युद्ध हो……….

काठमाडौं । यूरोपका सडकमा अहिले एउटा पुरानो गीत फेरि सुनिन थालेको छ । झन्डै डेढ सय वर्षअघि लेखिएको क्रान्तिकारी गीत- ‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल (International) । पेरिसमा प्रदर्शनकारीहरू एकै स्वरमा यो गीत गाइरहेका दृश्य सामाजिक सञ्जाल र अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय सञ्चारमाध्यममा सार्वजनिक भइरहेका छन्।

रातो झन्डा, विद्यार्थीका जुलुस, श्रमिक संगठनका प्रदर्शन र सरकारी नीतिविरुद्ध उठेका नाराबीच यो गीतको पुनरागमनले यूरोपको वर्तमान आन्दोलनलाई इतिहाससँग जोडेको छ ।

विद्यालयको अवस्था, बजेट कटौती र बढ्दो महँगीविरुद्ध देशव्यापी प्रदर्शन भइरहेका बेला माध्यमिक विद्यालयका विद्यार्थी, विश्वविद्यालयका विद्यार्थी तथा शिक्षक संगठनहरू आन्दोलनमा सहभागी भएका छन्।

फ्रान्सेली अधिकारीहरूका अनुसार पेरिसबाहिर मंगलबार दिउँसोसम्म १४० वटा प्रदर्शनमा ३२ हजार ८ सय मानिस सहभागी भएका थिए। सरकारले आन्दोलनमा ‘अति वामपन्थी’ समूहको संलग्नता रहेको आरोप लगाएको छ । डेढ सय वर्ष पुरानो कम्युनिस्ट गीत गाएका कारण सरकारले यस्तो आरोप लगाएको हो ।

‘कम्युनिस्ट इन्टरनेसनल’ श्रमिक एकता, सामाजिक समानता र शोषणविरुद्धको संघर्षको प्रतीक मानिने गीत हो। सन् १८७१ मा युजेन पोत्जिएले लेखेको यो गीत अहिले फेरि फ्रान्सका सडकमा गुञ्जिनुले वर्तमान आन्दोलनलाई ऐतिहासिक श्रमिक तथा क्रान्तिकारी संघर्षसँग जोडेको टिप्पणी गरिएको छ ।

महँगी, बेरोजगारी, आवास संकट, सार्वजनिक सेवामा बजेट कटौती र बढ्दो आर्थिक असमानताप्रति असन्तुष्ट नयाँ पुस्ताले विगतका क्रान्तिकारी प्रतीकलाई फेरि आफ्नो आन्दोलनको भाषाका रूपमा प्रयोग गरिरहेको संकेत यसलाई मानिएको छ ।

नोभेम्बरमा फ्रान्सका विभिन्न सहरमा सरकारको आर्थिक नीति, बजेट कटौती, जीवनयापनको बढ्दो खर्च र शिक्षा क्षेत्रको अवस्थाविरुद्ध प्रदर्शन भइरहेका छन्। कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी, श्रमिक संगठन, विद्यार्थी समूह र वामपन्थी संगठनहरू यी प्रदर्शनमा सहभागी छन्।

पेरिसको प्लास द ला रिपब्लिक (Place de la République) मा भएको प्रदर्शनमा सहभागीहरूले ऐतिहासिक क्रान्तिकारी गीत ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ सामूहिक रूपमा गाएको दृश्य सार्वजनिक भएको छ । यद्यपी यहाँ कम्युनिस्ट समूहभन्दा अन्य युवाहरूको सहभागिता बढी छ तर सबैले कम्युनिस्ट गीत गाएका छन् ।

यो गीत फ्रान्सेली कवि तथा क्रान्तिकारी युजेन पोत्जिए (Eugène Pottier) ले सन् १८७१ मा लेखेका थिए। त्यो समय फ्रान्सको इतिहासमा पेरिस कम्युनको छोटो तर प्रभावशाली क्रान्तिकारी प्रयोग भएको वर्ष थियो।

पोत्जिए पेरिस कम्युनका समर्थक थिए । पेरिसमा मजदुर र क्रान्तिकारीहरूले सत्ता सञ्चालनको वैकल्पिक संरचना निर्माण गरेको उक्त ऐतिहासिक घटनापछि उनले लेखेको गीत श्रमिक वर्गको एकता, शोषणविरुद्ध विद्रोह र समानतामूलक समाज निर्माणको आकांक्षासँग जोडियो ।

गीतका शब्द लेखिएको केही वर्षपछि सन् १८८८ मा पियरे देगेतेर (Pierre De Geyter) ले यसको संगीत तयार पारे । त्यसपछि ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ फ्रान्सबाट बाहिर फैलिँदै विश्वभरका समाजवादी, कम्युनिस्ट र श्रमिक आन्दोलनको साझा गीत बन्न पुग्यो । आज पनि नेपालसहित संसारभरका कम्युनिस्ट पार्टीका औपचारिक समारोहमा यो गान गाइन्छ ।

यसले श्रमिकलाई आफ्नो वर्गीय एकता सम्झाउने, पुरानो सत्ता संरचनाविरुद्ध उठ्न प्रेरित गर्ने र समानताको सपना व्यक्त गर्ने सांस्कृतिक प्रतीकको रूप लिएका थियो ।

सन् १८७१ को पेरिस कम्युन आधुनिक राजनीतिक इतिहासको एउटा महत्त्वपूर्ण घटना हो । फ्रान्स-प्रुस युद्धपछि पेरिसमा उत्पन्न राजनीतिक संकटका बीच मजदुर, राष्ट्रिय गार्ड र क्रान्तिकारी शक्तिहरूले शहरमा आफ्नै शासन व्यवस्था सञ्चालन गरेका थिए।

कम्युनले सामाजिक समानता, श्रमिकको अधिकार, धर्म र राज्यबीचको सम्बन्ध, सार्वजनिक सेवाको पुनर्संरचना तथा जनताको राजनीतिक सहभागिताजस्ता मुद्दा उठाएको थियो ।

तर त्यो शासन लामो समय टिकेन । फ्रान्सेली सरकारी सेनाले कम्युनलाई हिंसात्मक रूपमा दबायो । सन् १८७१ को मे महिनामा भएको दमनमा हजारौँ मानिस मारिए, गिरफ्तार भए वा निर्वासनमा पठाइए ।

पेरिस कम्युन त्यसपछि विश्वभरका समाजवादी र कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलनका लागि एउटा ऐतिहासिक सन्दर्भ बन्यो । आज पनि विभिन्न ठाउँमा कम्युनहरुको अभ्यास गरिन्छ । कार्ल मार्क्सले पनि यसलाई मजदुर वर्गले राजनीतिक सत्ता प्रयोग गर्ने ऐतिहासिक अनुभवका रूपमा विश्लेषण गरेका थिए ।

आज पेरिसमा ‘इन्टरनेसनल’ गाउनु र कम्युनको स्मरण गर्नु वर्तमान आन्दोलनलाई त्यही ऐतिहासिक संघर्षको निरन्तरताका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्ने प्रतीकात्मक प्रयास भएको फ्रान्सेली कविहरुले बताएका छन् ।

यूरोपका पछिल्ला आन्दोलनमा कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी, ट्रेड युनियन र विद्यार्थी संगठनहरूको सहभागिता उल्लेखनीय देखिएको छ । तर, प्रदर्शनमा सहभागी सबै युवा कम्युनिस्ट विचारधाराका अनुयायी हुन् भन्ने अर्थ लाग्दैन । किनकी यूरोपमा कम्युनिस्टहरूको संगठन अहिले त्यति निर्णायक मानिँदैन ।

अहिलेको आन्दोलनको प्रमुख आधार दैनिक जीवनसँग जोडिएका समस्या हुन् । महँगो घरभाडा, रोजगारीको असुरक्षा, बढ्दो मूल्य, सार्वजनिक शिक्षा र स्वास्थ्य सेवामा दबाब तथा सरकारको खर्च कटौती नीति।

यस्ता समस्यालाई पूँजीवादी अर्थव्यवस्थाको असमानता र श्रमिकमाथिको शोषणसँग जोडेर व्याख्या गर्ने वामपन्थी संगठनहरूले आफ्ना ऐतिहासिक नारालाई पुनः अगाडि ल्याएका छन्।

ग्रीसको राजधानी एथेन्समा पनि कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी अफ ग्रीस (KKE) र त्यससँग सम्बद्ध श्रमिक संगठन PAME को नेतृत्वमा विद्यार्थी तथा श्रमिकहरूले प्रदर्शन गरेका छन् ।

प्रदर्शनमा रातो झन्डा, श्रमिक अधिकारका नारा र सरकारी आर्थिक नीतिविरुद्ध आवाज उठाइएको छ। एथेन्सका सडकमा देखिएका यस्ता जुलुसले यूरोपको दक्षिणी भागमा पनि श्रमिक र विद्यार्थी संगठनहरू आर्थिक तथा राजनीतिक मुद्दामा सक्रिय रहेको देखाउँछन्।

ग्रीसको राजनीतिक इतिहासमा कम्युनिस्ट आन्दोलनको बलियो उपस्थिति रहँदै आएको छ। आर्थिक संकट, बेरोजगारी र मितव्ययिताको नाममा लागू गरिएका कठोर नीतिहरूले विगतमा पनि त्यहाँ ठूलो जनआन्दोलन जन्माएका थिए ।

अहिलेको प्रदर्शनमा पुराना क्रान्तिकारी प्रतीकहरूको प्रयोगले त्यही इतिहासलाई नयाँ पुस्तामाझ पुनः स्थापित गर्ने प्रयास गरेको देखिन्छ।

Kathmandu. An old song is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. The revolutionary song written almost 150 years ago - 'The Communist International'. Footage of protesters in Paris singing this song in unison is being made public on social media and international media. Amidst red flags, student marches, labor union demonstrations, and slogans raised against government policies, the song's return has connected Europe's current movements to history. As nationwide protests against school conditions, budget cuts, and rising inflation continue, secondary school students, university students, and teacher organizations have joined the movement. French authorities said 32,800 people had taken part in 140 demonstrations outside Paris by Tuesday afternoon. The government has accused the protests of being led by "far-left" groups, accusing them of singing a 150-year-old communist song. The Communist International is a song that symbolizes workers' unity, social equality, and the struggle against exploitation. Written by Eugene Potzier in 1871, this song is now resonating on the streets of France, connecting the current movement to historical workers' and revolutionary struggles. This is seen as a sign that a new generation, dissatisfied with inflation, unemployment, the housing crisis, budget cuts in public services, and growing economic inequality, is once again using the revolutionary symbols of the past as the language of their movement. Why was a 155-year-old song sung in Paris? In November, demonstrations are taking place in various cities across France against the government's economic policies, budget cuts, the rising cost of living, and the state of the education sector. The Communist Party, labor unions, student groups, and left-wing organizations are participating in these demonstrations. Footage has emerged of participants singing the historic revolutionary song 'The Internationale' en masse at a demonstration in Paris' Place de la République. Although the participation here is more from other youth groups than from communist groups, everyone is singing communist songs. This song was written by French poet and revolutionary Eugène Pottier in 1871. That was the year of the Paris Commune, a brief but influential revolutionary experiment in French history. Potzier was a supporter of the Paris Commune. After the historic event in which workers and revolutionaries created an alternative structure of power in Paris, the songs he wrote became associated with the unity of the working class, rebellion against exploitation, and aspirations for an egalitarian society. A few years after the lyrics were written, Pierre De Geyter composed the music for the song in 1888. The Internationale then spread beyond France and became a common anthem for socialist, communist, and labor movements around the world. Even today, the song is sung at official ceremonies of communist parties around the world, including Nepal. It took the form of a cultural symbol that reminded workers of their class unity, inspired them to rise up against the old power structure, and expressed the dream of equality. Why remember the Paris Commune? The Paris Commune of 1871 is a significant event in modern political history. Amid the political crisis that arose in Paris after the Franco-Prussian War, workers, National Guards, and revolutionary forces established their own government in the city. The commune raised issues such as social equality, workers' rights, the relationship between religion and state, the restructuring of public services, and the political participation of the people. But that rule did not last long. The French government troops violently suppressed the Commune. Thousands of people were killed, arrested, or sent into exile in the May 1871 crackdown. The Paris Commune then became a historical reference for socialist and communist movements around the world. Communes are still practiced in various places today. Karl Marx also analyzed it as a historical experience of the working class exercising political power. French poets have said that singing the 'Internationale' and remembering the Commune in Paris today is a symbolic attempt to present the current movement as a continuation of that historic struggle. Why are Marx's ideas on the streets again? The participation of communist parties, trade unions, and student organizations in recent movements in Europe has been notable. However, this does not mean that all the young people participating in the demonstrations are followers of communist ideology. Because the organization of communists in Europe is not considered to be that decisive at the moment. The main basis of the current movement is the problems related to daily life: high housing costs, job insecurity, rising prices, pressure on public education and health services, and government spending cuts. Leftist organizations that explain such problems by linking them to the inequality of the capitalist economy and the exploitation of workers have brought their historical slogans to the fore again. 'Communist International' is an influential symbol of that political language. The song conveys the message of transforming individual dissatisfaction into collective struggle. Therefore, singing this song in current demonstrations seems important in all three senses: the political direction of the movement, its connection to history, and its message of unity. March of communist students and workers in Athens Students and workers led by the Communist Party of Greece (KKE) and its affiliated labor organization PAME have also demonstrated in the Greek capital, Athens. The demonstrations, which have included red flags, workers' rights slogans and calls for a crackdown on government economic policies, are a sign that workers' and student organizations are also active on economic and political issues in southern Europe. The communist movement has had a strong presence in Greece's political history. Economic crisis, unemployment, and harsh policies implemented in the name of austerity have sparked large-scale popular movements there in the past. The use of old revolutionary symbols in the current demonstration appears to be an attempt to re-establish that same history among the new generation. From France to Spain: A common voice of economic discontent Reports of large demonstrations and strikes in France on November 5 and 17 have been released. There have been reports of a general strike in Spain on November 11, youth demonstrations in Italy, Germany and Belgium, and various forms of protests in more than 30 European countries. These movements are not all about the same issues. Some are against government budget cuts, others are for workers' wages and rights, others are against the housing crisis and inflation, and others are demanding improvements in education and public services. However, amidst these different issues, there is a common dissatisfaction - the feeling that the benefits of economic development are not reaching all sections of society equally and that the lives of ordinary citizens are becoming increasingly difficult. This discontent is being linked by left-wing organizations to questions of capitalism, class inequality, and labor exploitation. Therefore, the return of a historic song like the 'Internationale' to the demonstrations is seen not only as a cultural event but also as a political message. 155-year-old song, voice of a new generation The core message of the Communist International is the unity of workers and the collective struggle to change an unjust system. The song's famous lyrics call on workers to seek liberation from the old system and build their own future. For more than a century, this song has been the common anthem of communist movements, socialist parties, and labor organizations around the world. It has had a special place in national and political ceremonies in various countries, including the Soviet Union. In countries such as China, Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea, and Laos, communist regimes have given this song a place similar to the national anthem. Communist parties that have participated in central, provincial and local governments in countries including Nepal, India, Sri Lanka, Guinea, Cyprus, Peru and others at various times have sung the Communist International at their formal ceremonies. This song, written by Yutze Pottar in 1871, is probably the only song in the world that has been translated and set to music in the most languages. However, its return today does not only mean a desire to return to the political order of the past. Political analysts in Europe are commenting that it should also be understood as a cultural and political expression of the younger generation's attempt to connect their current dissatisfaction with historical struggles. The collective singing of protesters in videos from Paris that have spread on social media conveys the same message - even after decades of changing political systems, questions of economic inequality, workers' rights, and social justice have not gone away. The memory of the Paris Commune, the timeless ideas of Karl Marx, and the melody of the 'Communist International' are now being analyzed as a new crisis of capitalism, which is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. Whether this is a repetition of history or a new movement in which a new generation expresses its current dissatisfaction in the old revolutionary language - the political events of the coming days will answer that. The main basis of the current movement is the problems related to daily life: high housing costs, job insecurity, rising prices, pressure on public education and health services, and government spending cuts.

Leftist organizations that explain such problems by linking them to the inequality of the capitalist economy and the exploitation of workers have brought their historical slogans to the fore again.

'Communist International' is an influential symbol of that political language. The song conveys the message of transforming individual dissatisfaction into collective struggle. Therefore, singing this song in current demonstrations seems important in all three senses: the political direction of the movement, its connection to history, and its message of unity.

Students and workers led by the Communist Party of Greece (KKE) and its affiliated labor organization PAME have also demonstrated in the Greek capital, Athens.

The demonstrations, which have included red flags, workers' rights slogans and calls for a crackdown on government economic policies, are a sign that workers' and student organizations are also active on economic and political issues in southern Europe.

The communist movement has had a strong presence in Greece's political history. Economic crisis, unemployment, and harsh policies implemented in the name of austerity have sparked large-scale popular movements there in the past.

The use of old revolutionary symbols in the current demonstration appears to be an attempt to re-establish that same history among the new generation.

Reports of large demonstrations and strikes in France on November 5 and 17 have been released. There have been reports of a general strike in Spain on November 11, youth demonstrations in Italy, Germany and Belgium, and various forms of protests in more than 30 European countries.

These movements are not all about the same issues. Some are against government budget cuts, others are for workers' wages and rights, others are against the housing crisis and inflation, and others are demanding improvements in education and public services.

However, amidst these different issues, there is a common dissatisfaction - the feeling that the benefits of economic development are not reaching all sections of society equally and that the lives of ordinary citizens are becoming increasingly difficult.

This discontent is being linked by left-wing organizations to questions of capitalism, class inequality, and labor exploitation. Therefore, the return of a historic song like the 'Internationale' to the demonstrations is seen not only as a cultural event but also as a political message.

The core message of the Communist International is the unity of workers and the collective struggle to change an unjust system. The song's famous lyrics call on workers to seek liberation from the old system and build their own future.

For more than a century, this song has been the common anthem of communist movements, socialist parties, and labor organizations around the world. It has had a special place in national and political ceremonies in various countries, including the Soviet Union. In countries such as China, Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea, and Laos, communist regimes have given this song a place similar to the national anthem.

Communist parties that have participated in central, provincial and local governments in countries including Nepal, India, Sri Lanka, Guinea, Cyprus, Peru and others at various times have sung the Communist International at their formal ceremonies. This song, written by Yutze Pottar in 1871, is probably the only song in the world that has been translated and set to music in the most languages.

However, its return today does not only mean a desire to return to the political order of the past. Political analysts in Europe are commenting that it should also be understood as a cultural and political expression of the younger generation's attempt to connect their current dissatisfaction with historical struggles.

The collective singing of protesters in videos from Paris that have spread on social media conveys the same message - even after decades of changing political systems, questions of economic inequality, workers' rights, and social justice have not gone away.

The memory of the Paris Commune, the timeless ideas of Karl Marx, and the melody of the 'Communist International' are now being analyzed as a new crisis of capitalism, which is now being heard again on the streets of Europe. Whether this is a repetition of history or a new movement in which a new generation expresses its current dissatisfaction in the old revolutionary language - the political events of the coming days will answer that.
